quiz.title: חידון יישובים (Settlements quiz), Academy of the Hebrew Language

list.title: רשימת שמות היישובים בישראל (List of settlement names in Israel), Academy of the Hebrew Language, July 2022

groups.label: Say it right
groups.blurb: Places where the Academy's pronunciation isn't what you hear on the bus.

groups.label: Why it's called that
groups.blurb: Where the names come from. Some answers are not the obvious ones.

groups.label: Official spellings
groups.blurb: How the Academy writes the names in Latin letters, and the rules behind the odd ones.

groups.label: The full official name
groups.blurb: Towns whose official name is longer than the one on everyone's lips.

facts.head: Kfar SaVA, not Kfar SAba
facts.body: The city is named for a village mentioned in the Tosefta and the Talmud (Niddah 61a). There, סָבָא is the Aramaic word for 'grandfather', stressed on its last syllable and with no dagesh: it's not סַבָּא, the way you'd say Grandpa. Josephus wrote the name in Greek as Καφαρσαβα, with a single beta.

facts.head: Botsra, though everyone says Batsra
facts.body: The moshav next to Ra'anana is named for Basra in Iraq, where its founders fought as soldiers in the British army. Its Hebrew form, though, follows the biblical Botsra, a city in Edom. The qamats under the bet is a qamats katan, said 'o', so the standard pronunciation is Botsra, and that's also its official Latin spelling. Almost everyone says Batsra.

facts.head: Hefa, with a tsere
facts.body: The city appears in rabbinic literature (e.g. Shabbat 26a), and in every reading tradition we have it's חֵיפָה, with a tsere. That's the standard Hebrew pronunciation today too. חַיְפָה (Haifa) is the city's Arabic name, which is also the traditional Latin spelling the Academy keeps.

facts.head: Natsrat, not Natseret
facts.body: The city's official name is נָצְרַת, and so is Natsrat Illit's (now Nof HaGalil). Ancient Hebrew sources, especially early Land of Israel piyyut, put it in the same pattern as צָרְפַת, אָסְנַת and בָּשְׂמַת (a qamats gadol, then a vocal sheva). The Hebrew Language Committee recommended it, and the Academy still does. That said, Natseret also has ancient roots.

facts.head: Adummim, not Edomim
facts.body: The name comes from Joshua 15:7, which marks the border 'opposite the ascent of Adummim'. It probably refers to the reddish stones there. It has nothing to do with Edom. The dagesh in the mem is why the official Latin spelling has a double m.

facts.head: Yehud, not Yahud
facts.body: From the list of the tribe of Dan's cities in Joshua 19:45: 'וִיהֻד וּבְנֵי בְרַק וְגַת רִמּוֹן'. Yehud really does sit next to Bnei Brak, and there's a Gat Rimon nearby too. The vowel in וִיהֻד shows the yod has a sheva, just like וִירוּשָׁלַיִם.

facts.head: Holon, not Hulon
facts.body: Named for a city in Judah's territory mentioned in Joshua (21:15, 'וְאֶת חֹלֹן וְאֶת מִגְרָשֶׁהָ'), and fitting for a city built on shifting sand dunes (חוֹלוֹת). Compare Ramla, an Arabic name from raml, 'sand'.

facts.head: Shmona, not Shmone
facts.body: Named for eight men: Yosef Trumpeldor and seven comrades who fell defending nearby Tel Hai, most of them in the attack of 11 Adar 5680 (1920).

facts.head: Sderot, with a sin
facts.body: Founded as an immigrant transit camp in 1955 and named for a project planting avenues of trees (שְׂדֵרוֹת) along the roads. שְׂדֵרָה takes a sin, the left-dotted ש, and is related to סֵדֶר, 'order'.

facts.head: YotVAta, stress on the second syllable
facts.body: From Deuteronomy 10:7, 'יָטְבָתָה אֶרֶץ נַחֲלֵי מָיִם'. The place is Yotvat; the final heh means 'to' (like מִצְרַיְמָה, 'to Egypt'), so the stress stays on the -va-. The first qamats is a qamats katan, which is why it's Yot-, not Yat-.

facts.head: Yeroham, not Yeruham
facts.body: The town appears in the list of cities conquered by Pharaoh Shishak, and its name survives in the Arabic Tel Rakhma and Bir Rakhma. The vowels follow the biblical personal name יְרֹחָם, which appears several times in Tanakh.

facts.head: Yesud, not Yesod
facts.body: From Ezra 7:9, 'כִּי בְּאֶחָד לַחֹדֶשׁ הָרִאשׁוֹן הוּא יְסֻד הַמַּעֲלָה מִבָּבֶל': the start of the ascent from Babylon.

facts.head: Mikhmas, with a sin
facts.body: From 1 Samuel 13:5, where the Philistines 'encamped at Michmas'. Some link it to the root כמ"ס/כמ"ש, 'hidden' (as in כָּמוּס). The settlement Ma'ale Mikhmas carries the name.

facts.head: Tarum, not Tarom
facts.body: Tarum and its neighbor Ta'oz both take their names from Psalms 89:14, 'תָּעֹז יָדְךָ תָּרוּם יְמִינֶךָ'. The common 'Tarom' probably comes from rhyming it with Ta'oz.

facts.head: Named for one of Isaac's wells
facts.body: Not for Zechariah's streets full of children, and not for a kabbalist's book: Rehovot is the well Isaac dug that nobody quarreled over, 'וַיִּקְרָא שְׁמָהּ רְחֹבוֹת וַיֹּאמֶר כִּי עַתָּה הִרְחִיב ה׳ לָנוּ' (Genesis 26:22). The meeting where the name was chosen is described in the memoir of First Aliyah pioneer Yehiel Michel Pukhachevsky.

facts.head: A tribute to Los Angeles
facts.body: Not the prophet Malachi: the 'Town of Angels' honors the City of Angels, whose Jewish community gave generously to build it. Me'ammi, near Nahal Iron, works the same way: it honors the Jewish community of Miami.

facts.head: A translation of Herzl's novel
facts.body: Nahum Sokolow translated the title of Herzl's Altneuland ('Old New Land') as Tel Aviv: a tel is old, and aviv, spring, is new. The phrase is biblical, a place in Babylon where exiles from Judah lived: 'וָאָבוֹא אֶל הַגּוֹלָה תֵּל אָבִיב' (Ezekiel 3:15).

facts.head: Named for the emperor Tiberius
facts.body: The other explanations are rabbinic midrash on the name: it 'sits at the navel (טַבּוּר) of the Land of Israel', or 'its view is good (טוֹבָה רְאִיָּתָהּ)' (Megillah 6a). The official Latin form is Tverya; Tiberias is the traditional English name.

facts.head: A Canaanite god, a Greek god and an Arabic name, all at once
facts.body: The moshav by Herzliya is named for all of them. The Arabic Arsuf preserves the name of an ancient settlement named for the Canaanite god Reshef. In the Hellenistic period it was renamed Apollonia, for Apollo, the Greek god most like him.

facts.head: Arabic, plus 'the Valley'
facts.body: The name joins the Arabic al-Mujeidil ('little tower') to 'the Valley', meaning the Jezreel Valley. The other quiz answers have some truth in them too: the town sits on a high hill seen from all over the valley, and about twenty years after it was founded it built a tall tower, now on its emblem.

facts.head: Not 'peace': a man from Numbers
facts.body: It isn't named for a hope for peace on the Lebanese border. Shlomi is in the tribe of Asher's territory, and is named for the father of Asher's prince: 'וּלְמַטֵּה בְנֵי אָשֵׁר נָשִׂיא אֲחִיהוּד בֶּן שְׁלֹמִי' (Numbers 34:27). Moshav Ahihud was founded the same year, 1950.

facts.head: Three moshavim from one verse
facts.body: Ta'ashur, Brosh and Tidhar, north of Ofakim, all come from Isaiah 41:19: 'אָשִׂים בָּעֲרָבָה בְּרוֹשׁ תִּדְהָר וּתְאַשּׁוּר יַחְדָּו'. Following the verse's last word, they're called the 'Yahdav moshavim'.

facts.head: Hope, twice over
facts.body: Petah Tikva (1878) comes from Hosea 2:17, 'וְאֶת עֵמֶק עָכוֹר לְפֶתַח תִּקְוָה'. Nearby Mikve Israel (1870) comes from Jeremiah, 'מִקְוֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל מוֹשִׁיעוֹ בְּעֵת צָרָה', which plays on מִקְוֶה as both 'hope' and 'a gathering of water'.

facts.head: For the Gerrer Rebbe
facts.body: Founded by Poalei Agudat Israel, it's named for Rabbi Avraham Mordechai (רא"ם) Alter, the third Gerrer Rebbe. The phrasing is from Psalms 29:6, 'וְשִׂרְיֹן כְּמוֹ בֶן רְאֵמִים'.

facts.head: It was 'Radar Hill'
facts.body: The town is named for the hill it was built on, known as Radar Hill. The name was a mistake: a British relay station on top looked like radar. Hebraized, הָרָדָאר became הַר אֲדָר.

facts.head: For India, in biblical dress
facts.body: The moshav near Ashkelon is named for India (הֹדּוּ), where its first settlers came from. Its form is the biblical personal name הוֹדִיָּה, from Caleb ben Yefuneh's descendants.

facts.head: A Talmudic town, maybe a Roman fort
facts.body: The Sharon moshav carries the name of a town from the Talmud: Burgata in the Yerushalmi, Barketa in the Bavli. Some identify it with nearby Burj al-Atut. The name may come from the Latin burgus, 'a fort' or 'a small watchtower'.

facts.head: A watering trough
facts.body: A רַהַט is a trough for watering flocks, named for the sheep and goats of the city's Bedouin founders.

facts.head: Hebrew for Yajur
facts.body: The kibbutz near Haifa got a Hebrew form of the place's Arabic name, Yajur.

facts.head: Officially Ra'ananna, with a double n
facts.body: The Academy's transliteration doubles a letter that has a strong dagesh, and רַעֲנַנָּה has one in its last nun. The apostrophe stands for the ayin. Other doubled letters: Ma'ale Adummim, Rosh Pinna, Tsur Hadassa, Mevasseret Tsiyon, Ganne Tikva, Kinneret, Abbirim.

facts.head: Elat, not Eilat
facts.body: The tsere is written as a plain e, so the official Latin form is Elat, just as it's Bet Shemesh and En Gedi, not Beit Shemesh and Ein Gedi.

facts.head: Bne Brak, not Bnei Brak
facts.body: The tsere at the end of בְּנֵי is also just e. You'll see Bne Re'em and Avne Etan written the same way.

facts.head: Kesarya, not Caesarea
facts.body: Unlike Jerusalem, Haifa or Nazareth, Caesarea gets no traditional exception: its official Latin form is a straight transliteration, Kesarya. Tiberias is Tverya.

facts.head: The six names that keep their old spellings
facts.body: A few names aren't transliterated but kept in their customary spelling: Jerusalem, Tel Aviv–Yafo, Nazareth, Haifa, Safed (צְפַת) and Acre (עַכּוֹ).

facts.head: Only six names get a stress mark
facts.body: Of more than 1,300 names, the list's vowel-pointed column marks the stress on just six, all of them Arabic: Mi'ilya (מֶ֫עֶלְיַא, stressed on the first syllable), Sulam, Kabul, Ibtin, I'billin and 'Arraba. Every Hebrew name, Kfar Sava included, is left to the usual rules of vowel pointing.

facts.head: Het gets a line under the h
facts.body: In the official spellings, het is h̠, an h with a line under it (H̠adera, Reh̠ovot, H̠olon), to tell it apart from heh. Where a sign can't show the line, the Academy says to separate letter pairs with an apostrophe instead, so they don't read as sh, th or kh: Yits'hak, Bit'ha, Mak'hul.

facts.head: The Academy spells the names. It doesn't pick them.
facts.body: In its own words, the Academy doesn't decide the names themselves: that's the job of the Government Names Committee. The Academy's list gives each name four ways, in full Hebrew spelling, vowel-pointed, in Arabic, and in Latin letters, so that road signs, ministries and newsrooms all spell it the same way.

facts.head: Tel Aviv–Yafo
facts.body: The city has officially included Jaffa since the two merged in 1950.

facts.head: Yehud–Monosson
facts.body: Yehud and the neighboring Neve Monosson are one municipality, and the official name carries both.

facts.head: Kokhav Ya'ir–Tsur Yig'al
facts.body: One local council, two names, both in the official name.

facts.head: Kadima–Tsoran
facts.body: Kadima and Tsoran merged, and the Academy's spelling for both halves is in the official name.

facts.head: Pardes Hanna–Karkur
facts.body: The dagesh in חַנָּה gives the official spelling a double n: Pardes H̠anna.

facts.head: Binyamina–Giv'at Ada
facts.body: Two First Aliyah-era moshavot, one name.

facts.head: Modi'in–Makkabbim–Re'ut
facts.body: Three names, and the Academy doubles both the k and the b in Makkabbim.

facts.head: Ma'alot–Tarshiha
facts.body: A joint Jewish and Arab municipality in the western Galilee, with both towns in its name.
